contentBlocks.body: A Result<T, E> type makes success and failure part of a function's signature instead of hiding failure in a thrown exception. Written generically, one small set of helpers works for every Result in the app: parsing, saving, validating.

Notice that mapResult can return the failed result unchanged: a { ok: false; error: E } is a valid Result<U, E> for any U, because it carries no value. The discriminant check result.ok is what makes that safe.

Two ways to combine many results come up constantly. Fail fast stops at the first error, which suits a pipeline where later steps depend on earlier ones. Collect all gathers every error, which suits forms and batch imports, where the user wants to fix everything in one go.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Why is Result<never, E> assignable to Result<number, E>?

choices: never is the same as any
It is not assignable; it needs a cast
never is assignable to every type, so the ok branch fits any T
payload.answer: never is assignable to every type, so the ok branch fits any T
payload.explanation: never is the bottom type. A value of type never can be used where any other type is expected, which is what makes err() usable everywhere.

knowledgeItems.prompt: A signup form validates five fields. Which combining strategy gives the best user experience?

choices: Collect all errors and show them together
Throw an exception from the first validator
payload.answer: Collect all errors and show them together
payload.explanation: Fail fast suits dependent steps; independent field checks should all run so the user can fix everything at once.

payload.text: A helper that transforms the value inside a successful Result and passes failures through unchanged is usually called ____Result.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Combine a list of Result<T, E> values: all ok returns { ok: true, value: T[] }, otherwise { ok: false, errors: E[] } with every error in order.
